narrative: Fire remained a recurring signal this cycle: a 35-year chronosequence in Ecology found aboveground nitrogen pools still rebuilding while deeper pools stay flat after stand-replacing fire, and a seasonally dry subtropical study showed post-fire vegetation carrying a structural legacy that outlasts floristic recovery. Climate's fingerprint showed up unevenly across taxa - century-long herbarium records revealed season-dependent shifts in tropical flowering phenology, a common lizard showed strong thermal plasticity but low heritability in breeding timing, and overwintering strategy, not temperature alone, set the direction of long-term body-mass change in northern mammals. Movement and behaviour papers converged on landscape context: boreal and alpine pygmy owls differ in home-range size with photoperiod and forest structure, individual boldness structured spatial encounters in a rodent community, and strong social bonds predicted survival in a cooperative bird. On the trophic side, wolves and people both shaped deer browsing pressure in a Central European forest, and a 24-year dataset linked climate-driven resource shifts to owl-prey interaction strength. Herbivory and symbiosis findings pointed to overlooked players: ant exclusion, not plant chemistry, explained why phylogenetic distance predicted herbivory in exotic oaks, and a four-country metagenomic survey found Frankia strains far more diverse in Casuarina nodules than cultured isolates suggested. Urban ecology and evolution themes linked up: plumage polymorphism tracked climate and urbanisation gradients across cities globally, and white clover's adaptive trajectory in urban environments depended on its biogeographic origin. Methods contributions this cycle leaned toward monitoring at scale, including new tools for edge-AI biodiversity sensing and individual bird identification from bioacoustic embeddings.
